title: New Jerusalem Prophecy
summary: Isaiah pictures Jerusalem within a renewed creation: people build homes, enjoy the work of their hands, and live without the familiar losses of early death and danger. Revelation 21 retells that hope as a holy city descending from God, where death, grief, and pain are gone and God dwells with humanity. The images overlap, but Revelation gives its own vision and does not simply repeat every detail from Isaiah. Ezekiel 40:1–4 introduces a temple vision from exile; these opening verses establish its setting, not the details of the city itself.
historical_context: The cited passages come from different literary settings. Isaiah 65–66 speaks of a renewed Jerusalem and creation through prophetic images of lasting life, worship, and judgment. Ezekiel 40:1–4 dates the opening of a temple vision to the twenty-fifth year of exile and describes the visionary setting; the cited verses do not yet describe the temple plan. Revelation 21 presents a later Christian vision of the holy city coming from God. The references do not establish one shared date or a step-by-step timetable for these images.
literary_context: Isaiah 65:17–25 moves from the promise of new heavens and a new earth to everyday pictures of security and flourishing: building, planting, long life, and peace among creatures. Isaiah 66:22–24 holds the permanence of the new creation beside worship and a stark image of judgment. Revelation 21:1–27 reuses creation and city imagery, describing the city’s arrival, God’s presence, the end of death and grief, and the nations’ place in its light. Ezekiel 40:1–4 is a vision-opening, not a description of the city; its role here is limited to introducing Ezekiel’s later temple vision.
covenantal_significance: These visions describe restoration as shared life in God’s presence, not simply a change of location. Isaiah makes the hope concrete through safe homes, fruitful labor, and life no longer cut short; Revelation emphasizes God dwelling with humanity and the end of death, mourning, and pain. Both preserve judgment alongside hope, and Revelation also pictures the nations walking by the city’s light. The texts invite readers to connect restoration, creation, and divine presence while leaving the precise relation among their images open.
canonical_role: New Jerusalem Prophecy serves as a prophetic anchor, connecting oracle context, canonical development, and related fulfillment or restoration themes.

interpretive_notes.note: Read the oracle first in its own historical setting.
Prophetic speech is covenantal proclamation before it is prediction.
